title: IMMUNODEFICIENCY 35
alt_titles: HYPER-IgE SYNDROME WITH ATYPICAL MYCOBACTERIOSIS, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE
HIES WITH ATYPICAL MYCOBACTERIOSIS, AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene (176941) on chromosome 19p13.2.

checks.claim: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Combined with the reported TYK2 deficiency cases, we summary the main features of TYK2 deficiency: (a) TYK2 gene mutation; (b) Autosomal recessive inheritance;
checks.explanation: The paper describes TYK2 deficiency (IMD35) as autosomal recessive. Its own patient has a homozygous mutation (c.2395G>A, p.G799R), and Table 3 lists compound heterozygous cases from the literature (Nemoto, c.209_212del/c.691C>T). The paper says 'TYK2 deficiency' rather than 'IMD35', which is just a different name for the same disorder.

checks.claim: The TYK2 gene is located on chromosome 19p13.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Tyrosine kinase 2 (Tyk2) is a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase that belongs to the Janus kinase (Jak) family.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the chromosomal location. It is accepted here only as standard nomenclature added to the gene the paper studies.

paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency (Kilic et al., 2012) caused by tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2) deficiency (Minegishi et al., 2006). The first reported patient had unusual susceptibility to mycobacteria and viruses and had features of hyper-IgE syndrome, including atopic dermatitis and elevated serum IgE (Minegishi et al., 2006). TYK2-deficient patients reported later did not have hyper-IgE syndrome (Kreins et al., 2015). The cellular defect includes impaired responses to IL-12 and type I interferons, which require TYK2 for signaling (Minegishi et al., 2006).

checks.claim: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: The first patient with autosomal recessive (AR) tyrosine kinase 2 (Tyk2) deficiency, was reported in 2006.
checks.explanation: The paper describes TYK2 deficiency as an autosomal recessive immunodeficiency; the patient is homozygous and has infectious susceptibility. 'IMD35' is the standard OMIM name for this disorder.

checks.claim: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by tyrosine kinase-2 (TYK2) deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: Thus, the Tyk2 deficiency is likely to account for the patient's complex clinical manifestations
checks.explanation: The paper links the patient's disease to Tyk2 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) reported 7 further TYK2-deficient patients from 5 families of 4 different ethnic groups. The patients had mycobacterial disease (BCG and/or tuberculosis) and/or viral disease. None had hyper-IgE syndrome or high serum IgE. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that hyper-IgE syndrome is not a consistent feature of TYK2 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: IMD35 is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern (Kreins et al., 2015). Minegishi et al. (2006) and Kreins et al. (2015) found homozygous TYK2 mutations in affected individuals.

checks.evidence_quote: Thus, the seven patients from five kindreds reported here probably had autosomal recessive (AR) TYK2 deficiency
checks.explanation: AR inheritance stated (the paper hedges it as 'probably').

checks.claim: Minegishi et al. (2006) found homozygous TYK2 mutations in individuals affected with TYK2 deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient
checks.explanation: Minegishi et al. reported one patient with one homozygous mutation, not several affected individuals. The plural 'mutations' and 'individuals' overstates what this paper found.

checks.evidence_quote: We identified homozygous mutations in TYK2 by linkage analysis and Sanger sequencing (P2), WES (P3 to P7), or targeted NGS (P8).

paragraphs.text: In a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome, Minegishi et al. (2006) found a homozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene. The patient's cells had defective signaling in response to several cytokines, including type I interferons, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-23, and showed accelerated Th2 differentiation. Minegishi et al. (2006) concluded that TYK2 deficiency was likely to account for the patient's complex clinical manifestations, including impaired Th1 differentiation and accelerated Th2 differentiation.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) found homozygous null mutations in TYK2 in further patients with TYK2 deficiency. TYK2 protein was undetectable in cells from all of the patients. The patients' cells had impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta, with reduced IFN-gamma production, and also had impaired responses to IL-23 and IL-10. Responses to IL-6 were normal, as were responses to IL-21, IL-27, IFN-gamma, IL-28/29 (IFN-lambda), and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF). Responses to IFN-alpha, IL-12, IL-23, and IL-10 were equally impaired in all TYK2-deficient patients, including the first patient, so only the IL-6 response differed from that patient. Kreins et al. (2015) attributed the lack of hyper-IgE syndrome in their patients to their normal IL-6 responses. They concluded that the IL-10 and IL-23 defects were unlikely to be the cause of hyper-IgE syndrome in the first patient.

checks.evidence_quote: We identified seven other TYK2-deficient patients from five families and four different ethnic groups. These patients were homozygous for one of five null mutations, different from that seen in P1.

checks.explanation: Holds for the seven newly reported patients; the first patient (P1) was hyporesponsive to IL-6.

checks.claim: Cells from the TYK2-deficient patients had normal responses to IL-21, IL-27, IFN-gamma, IL-28/29 (IFN-lambda), and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF).
checks.evidence_quote: Cellular responses to IL-21, IL-27, IFN-γ, IL-28/29 (IFN-λ), and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) were normal.

checks.claim: Responses to IFN-alpha, IL-12, IL-23, and IL-10 were equally impaired in all TYK2-deficient patients, including the first reported TYK2-deficient patient.
checks.evidence_quote: given that the response to the cytokines IFN-α, IL-12, IL-23, and IL-10 are equally impaired in all TYK2-deficient patients (including P1)

checks.claim: The IL-6 response was the only response in which the newly reported TYK2-deficient patients differed from the first reported TYK2-deficient patient.
checks.evidence_quote: Response to IL-6 | impaired | normal | normal | normal | normal | normal | normal | normal | normal
checks.explanation: Among the cytokine responses compared, only the IL-6 response differed. But the paper does not call it the only difference: it says other biological differences are at work and that 'a role for other pathways (not studied here) cannot be ruled out.'

checks.claim: Kreins et al. (2015) attributed the absence of hyper-IgE syndrome in their TYK2-deficient patients to normal IL-6 responses.
checks.evidence_quote: The leukocytes and fibroblasts of all seven newly identified TYK2-deficient patients, unlike those of P1, responded normally to IL-6, possibly accounting for the lack of HIES in these patients.
checks.explanation: The paper offers this only as a possibility ('possibly accounting'). It also concludes that P1's IL-6 defect does not depend on TYK2 and that HIES is not an intrinsic feature of TYK2 deficiency. The draft states the attribution without this hedge.

checks.claim: Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the IL-10 and IL-23 response defects were unlikely to cause hyper-IgE syndrome in the first reported TYK2-deficient patient.
checks.evidence_quote: given that the response to the cytokines IFN-α, IL-12, IL-23, and IL-10 are equally impaired in all TYK2-deficient patients (including P1), defects in these responses are unlikely to be the cause of HIES in P1.
checks.explanation: The paper reaches this conclusion for IL-10 and IL-23, and also for IFN-alpha and IL-12.
